turns.content: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today?

Doctor: Hello, I’m your doctor today. What brings you in today? Patient: I’ve had a sudden rash starting last night on the upper half of my back, and I’m really concerned because I don’t remember any new exposures like detergents or plants. I’ve also had a new cough and some mouth sores.

[REASONING]
Key findings so far: sudden onset rash on upper back starting last night; no clear new exposures; associated new cough and mouth sores. This combination raises concern for a mucocutaneous process (e.g., severe drug reaction or viral exanthem), and less likely for isolated contact dermatitis.
Top candidates (tentative):
1) Steven-Johnson syndrome — mucosal involvement (mouth sores) plus rash; often triggered by a medication exposure (may not be recognized immediately).
2) Toxic exposure — could cause acute rash with respiratory symptoms and mucosal irritation depending on agent.
3) Bed bug bite — can cause sudden localized rash, but mouth sores and cough are less typical.
4) Histoplasmosis — can cause cough and oral lesions, but rash starting overnight is less typical.
5) Acute lymphoblastic leukemia — can present with systemic symptoms and mucosal issues, but sudden overnight rash is less characteristic.
Most informative next question: determine whether there was any new medication (especially antibiotics, anticonvulsants, NSAIDs) in the past 1–3 weeks, since that strongly discriminates SJS/TEN and other drug reactions.
[/REASONING]
What new medications (including antibiotics, anti-seizure meds, NSAIDs like ibuprofen/naproxen, or over-the-counter supplements) have you started in the last 1–3 weeks?

Patient: I started new arthritis management with my primary care provider a bit recently, but I can’t recall the exact name of the medication. I also haven’t taken any antibiotics, seizure medicines, or new OTC pain relievers like ibuprofen or naproxen.

[REASONING]
Key findings so far: sudden rash on upper back since last night; new cough and mouth sores; no antibiotics, seizure meds, or new NSAIDs/OTC pain relievers; started a new arthritis medication recently but patient can’t recall name.
Top candidates:
1) Steven-Johnson syndrome — still possible because many arthritis meds (e.g., allopurinol, NSAIDs, sulfonamides, some biologics) can trigger SJS; mucosal involvement (mouth sores) supports.
2) Toxic exposure — still possible if the arthritis med was a new agent or if there was an environmental exposure; mucosal involvement can occur.
3) Acute viral exanthem (not in provided list) — cough + mouth sores could fit viral illness, but the sudden rash with mucosal lesions keeps SJS high.
4) Bed bug bite — sudden rash possible, but mouth sores/cough are less consistent.
5) Histoplasmosis — cough + oral lesions possible, but abrupt overnight rash is less typical.
Most informative next question: ask about the rash appearance and mucosal/skin severity (blistering, skin pain, peeling, eye involvement). This discriminates SJS/TEN from benign exanthems/contact reactions.
[/REASONING]
Is the rash painful or burning, and have you noticed any blistering, skin peeling, or sores/irritation in your eyes (redness, gritty feeling, discharge)?

Doctor: Is the rash painful or burning, and have you noticed any blistering, skin peeling, or sores/irritation in your eyes (redness, gritty feeling, discharge)? Patient: It feels burning and uncomfortable, and I’ve started to have mouth sores that are quite tender; I’m not sure about blistering or peeling yet, and I haven’t noticed eye irritation.

[REASONING]
Key findings so far: burning rash starting last night on upper back; tender mouth sores; no eye symptoms yet; no known antibiotics/NSAIDs/anticonvulsants; started new arthritis medication recently (name unknown).
Top candidates:
1) Steven-Johnson syndrome — burning pain + mucosal involvement (tender mouth sores) strongly supports; early course may not yet have peeling/blistering or eye findings.
2) Toxic exposure — can cause burning rash and mucosal irritation, but less likely without a clear exposure history.
3) Bed bug bite — typically itchy rather than burning and usually not associated with mouth sores/cough.
4) Histoplasmosis — can cause oral lesions and cough, but acute burning rash overnight is less typical.
5) Acute lymphoblastic leukemia — can cause mucositis and rash, but sudden onset overnight is less typical.
Most informative next question: determine timing and whether the rash started within days to ~2–8 weeks of starting the arthritis medication (SJS often occurs 1–3 weeks after a new drug, sometimes sooner with re-exposure).
[/REASONING]
When did you start the arthritis medication relative to the rash onset (how many days ago), and did you take any dose before the rash started?
Patient: I can’t say for sure, but I think the new arthritis medication was started about a week or so before the rash. I took at least one dose before the rash started.

[REASONING]
Key findings so far: burning rash on upper back since last night; tender mouth sores; no eye symptoms yet; new arthritis medication started ~1 week before rash; at least one dose before onset; no antibiotics/NSAIDs/anticonvulsants.
Top candidates:
1) Steven-Johnson syndrome — classic temporal relationship (often 1–3 weeks after starting a high-risk drug) plus mucosal involvement and burning pain.
2) Toxic exposure — could cause mucosal symptoms, but less supported without exposure details.
3) Acute viral illness with exanthem — cough + mouth sores, but burning rash and drug timing favor SJS.
4) Acute myelogenous leukemia / acute lymphoblastic leukemia — mucositis/rash possible, but the tight drug timing and acute onset make SJS more likely.
5) Histoplasmosis — can cause oral lesions and cough, but acute overnight rash is less typical.
Most informative next question: ask about any skin tenderness/rapid spread and whether there are target lesions or purpura; also ask if any rash is on face/eyes/genitals/hands/feet. This helps gauge severity and SJS/TEN vs other causes.
[/REASONING]
Has the rash spread beyond the upper back (e.g., face, chest, groin/genitals, hands/feet), and are there any dark spots/purple areas or widespread skin tenderness?

Doctor: Has the rash spread beyond the upper back (e.g., face, chest, groin/genitals, hands/feet), and are there any dark spots/purple areas or widespread skin tenderness? Patient: It’s still mostly on my upper back, but it feels tender and sore where it is, and I haven’t noticed dark purple spots. I haven’t seen it on my face, hands, feet, or genitals, and I don’t have eye or vision symptoms.

[REASONING]
Key findings so far: burning/tender rash localized mostly to upper back; tender mouth sores; cough; no eye symptoms; no purpura/dark spots; no spread to face/hands/feet/genitals. Started new arthritis medication ~1 week prior; took at least one dose before rash.
Top candidates:
1) Steven-Johnson syndrome — still plausible due to mucosal involvement (mouth sores) and burning pain with drug timing; however, lack of spread/purpura and no eye involvement makes it less classic (could be early/milder SJS or another mucocutaneous drug reaction).
2) Toxic exposure — can cause burning rash and mucosal irritation; less supported because no exposure identified.
3) Acute viral exanthem — cough + mouth sores could be viral, but burning pain and drug timing keep drug reaction high.
4) Bed bug bite — sudden rash but would be itchy and localized; mouth sores/cough argue against.
5) Acute myelogenous leukemia / acute lymphoblastic leukemia — mucositis/rash possible, but acute overnight onset and drug timing favor SJS over malignancy.
Most informative next question: ask about fever and any flu-like prodrome (fever, malaise) and whether the mouth sores are ulcerations vs just irritation—this helps separate SJS from viral causes.
[/REASONING]

Doctor: Have you had a fever (measured or felt), chills, or just generally feeling ill before or since the rash started? Also, are the mouth sores true ulcers/bleeding or just irritation? Patient: I haven’t had a fever or chills, and I haven’t felt sick otherwise—just the rash burning and the mouth sores, which are pretty painful and seem like ulcers.

[REASONING]
Key findings so far: afebrile, no chills or systemic illness; sudden burning tender rash mostly upper back; painful mouth ulcers; no eye symptoms; no purpura; started new arthritis medication ~1 week prior; no known antibiotics/NSAIDs/anticonvulsants.
Top candidates:
1) Steven-Johnson syndrome — mucosal ulceration (mouth sores) + burning pain + temporal relationship to new drug (~1 week) strongly supports even without fever/skin spread yet.
2) Toxic exposure — can cause mucosal ulcerations and burning rash, but no exposure identified; less likely than drug reaction given timing.
3) Acute viral illness with mucositis/exanthem — mouth ulcers and cough could fit, but absence of fever/prodrome and drug timing make it less likely.
4) Bed bug bite — unlikely due to mouth ulcers and burning pain.
5) Acute myelogenous leukemia / acute lymphoblastic leukemia — mucositis can occur, but sudden localized burning rash with drug timing makes malignancy less likely.
Most informative next question: ask whether the patient has any history of prior similar reactions to medications and specifically whether the arthritis med could be allopurinol or a sulfonamide/antibiotic-like drug (even if they don’t know name). Also ask if they have any new meds besides that one (including herbal). This is discriminating for SJS risk.
[/REASONING]

Also, did you start any other new meds or herbal supplements around the same time? Patient: I’ve never had anything like this with medications before. I’m not sure what the arthritis medicine is, and I didn’t start any other new medications or supplements that I can recall.

[REASONING]
Key findings so far: first-time episode; sudden burning rash (mostly upper back) with painful mouth ulcers; cough; no fever/chills; no eye symptoms; started an unknown arthritis medication about a week before onset; no other new meds/supplements; no known antibiotic/NSAID/sulfa exposure.
Top candidates:
1) Steven-Johnson syndrome — still most likely due to mucosal ulceration + burning rash + close timing to new medication, even if localized and without fever/eye involvement.
2) Toxic exposure — possible given lack of clear medication name/exposure history; mucosal involvement can occur.
3) Acute viral illness with mucositis/exanthem — cough + mouth ulcers could be viral, but burning pain and drug timing argue against.
4) Acute myelogenous leukemia / acute lymphoblastic leukemia — mucositis/rash possible but less consistent with abrupt onset and medication timing.
5) Bed bug bite — unlikely due to mouth ulcers and cough.
Most informative next question: ask about current ability to swallow, hydration status, and any genital sores or inability to eat/drink—severity assessment and additional mucosal sites for SJS.
[/REASONING]
Are you able to swallow and drink normally, and have you noticed any sores on your lips/inside cheeks/throat or anywhere else (including genitals)?

Doctor: Are you able to swallow and drink normally, and have you noticed any sores on your lips/inside cheeks/throat or anywhere else (including genitals)? Patient: Swallowing is uncomfortable but I can still drink some; the mouth sores are mainly inside my mouth, and I haven’t noticed any genital sores.

[REASONING]
Key findings so far: afebrile; burning tender rash mostly upper back; painful internal mouth ulcers; uncomfortable swallowing but still able to drink; cough; no eye symptoms; no genital lesions; started unknown arthritis medication ~1 week prior; first-time reaction; no other new meds/exposures known.
Top candidates:
1) Steven-Johnson syndrome — mucosal ulceration + burning rash with recent high-risk drug timing remains most consistent; incomplete classic distribution/eye findings can occur early or with milder spectrum.
2) Toxic exposure — can cause mucocutaneous injury with oral ulcers and rash; less supported by lack of exposure history.
3) Acute viral illness with mucositis/exanthem — mouth ulcers and cough could fit, but burning drug-timed rash makes this less likely.
4) Acute myelogenous leukemia / acute lymphoblastic leukemia — mucositis/rash possible but abrupt onset and medication timing favor SJS.
5) Bed bug bite — unlikely due to mouth ulcers and cough.
Most informative next question: ask about any difficulty breathing, wheezing/stridor, or lip/tongue swelling (airway involvement) and whether there is any rapid progression over hours (severity/urgency).
[/REASONING]
Do you have any trouble breathing, wheezing/stridor, or swelling of your lips/tongue, and has the rash been rapidly worsening over the last several hours?

Doctor: Do you have any trouble breathing, wheezing/stridor, or swelling of your lips/tongue, and has the rash been rapidly worsening over the last several hours? Patient: My breathing feels okay, no wheezing or throat swelling, and my lips and tongue don’t seem swollen; the rash has stayed about the same, though the burning discomfort is pretty strong.

[REASONING]
Key findings so far: burning/tender rash mostly upper back (not spreading to face/hands/genitals), painful internal mouth ulcers, cough; afebrile; no eye symptoms; no lip/tongue swelling; breathing okay; rash stable over hours; started unknown arthritis medication ~1 week prior; no prior similar reactions; no other new meds/exposures known.
Top candidates:
1) Steven-Johnson syndrome — mucosal ulceration + burning rash with close timing to new medication; lack of fever/eye involvement and limited distribution could indicate early or milder SJS spectrum.
2) Toxic exposure — can mimic SJS with mucosal injury and rash, but less supported without exposure history.
3) Acute viral illness with mucositis/exanthem — cough + mouth ulcers possible; however burning pain and drug timing favor SJS.
4) Acute myelogenous leukemia / acute lymphoblastic leukemia — mucositis/rash possible, but abrupt onset and medication association make malignancy less likely.
5) Bed bug bite — sudden rash possible but mouth ulcers and burning are atypical.
Most informative next action: ask about any current use of high-risk drugs commonly used for arthritis/gout (allopurinol/febuxostat, NSAIDs, sulfonamides) and whether the patient has a history of gout or kidney disease; this may identify the likely trigger for SJS.
[/REASONING]

Also, is the skin there painful to touch? Patient: It’s made up of burning red patches that feel very sore to touch, and I haven’t seen any blisters or skin peeling yet.
